summary: Defines LEDBAT, an experimental congestion control algorithm for background traffic. It watches changes in one-way delay to detect queues building up, and uses spare bandwidth while backing off quickly so it does not slow down other traffic on the path.

plainLanguage.summary: Low Extra Delay Background Transport (LEDBAT) is designed for large transfers that should not interfere with other traffic. It estimates queueing delay from timestamps and reduces its sending rate when delay exceeds its target.

subtitle: An experimental congestion-control algorithm for background transfers that should yield to competing traffic.

tldr.problem: Background transfers need network capacity but should add little delay for interactive traffic sharing the same bottleneck.
tldr.mechanism: LEDBAT measures one-way delay and adjusts its congestion window based on estimated queueing delay relative to a target.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines an Experimental algorithm and identifies parameters and network effects that require further evaluation.

facts.label: Loss response
facts.value: Halve congestion window at most once per RTT

today: RFC 6817 is Experimental, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC identifies parameter values, filters, framing, and network effects as areas for further experimentation.

sections.title: Goals for Background Traffic
sections.content:
Standard TCP congestion control seeks to share bottleneck bandwidth among flows. Some background applications, such as software updates and file transfers, instead aim to use available capacity while interfering as little as possible with delay-sensitive applications.

LEDBAT is a delay-based congestion-control mechanism for this purpose. Its goals are to use available bandwidth when other traffic is absent, add limited queueing delay when traffic is present, and yield quickly to standard TCP flows.
sections.plainLanguage: LEDBAT is intended for transfers that can wait. It uses spare capacity and aims to reduce its impact when other flows compete for the same link.

sections.title: Where LEDBAT Can Be Used
sections.content:
LEDBAT can be implemented in a transport protocol or an application if the data path can carry timestamps and acknowledge data frequently. The RFC discusses use with TCP, SCTP, and DCCP, as well as application protocols built on UDP.

With an ECN-capable framing protocol, LEDBAT should react to an ECN mark as it would to loss. Active Queue Management and Weighted Fair Queuing can change how LEDBAT competes with other flows.
sections.plainLanguage: LEDBAT needs timestamps in data and regular acknowledgements. It can be used with several transport protocols or application protocols that provide those functions.

sections.title: How Delay Controls the Sending Rate
sections.content:
Each data segment carries a sender timestamp. The receiver compares it with its own clock, then returns the measured one-way delay in an acknowledgement. The sender estimates the base delay from recent minimum measurements and estimates queueing delay as the difference between current and base delay.

The sender adjusts its congestion window in proportion to the difference between queueing delay and the target. Below the target, the window grows; above it, the window shrinks. On data loss, the sender halves the window at most once per round-trip time. If no acknowledgement arrives within the congestion timeout, it reduces the window to one MSS and backs off the timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender compares current delay with the lowest recent delay to estimate queueing. It increases its window below the target and reduces it above the target.

sections.title: Parameter Values and Measurement
sections.content:
The target queueing delay must be 100 milliseconds or less, and gain must be 1 or less. The base-delay history should keep ten one-minute minima. Initial and minimum congestion windows should both be 2, and must not exceed the corresponding TCP values.

The sender may filter recent delay samples to reduce noise, but the filter must remain responsive to persistent congestion. Clock offset cancels when queueing delay is computed, while clock skew can accumulate error. The RFC suggests possible skew-correction approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC limits the target delay and gain so LEDBAT does not ramp up too aggressively. It also describes how sample filtering and clock errors affect delay estimates.

sections.title: Competition and Open Questions
sections.content:
When its delay estimate is zero, LEDBAT increases its congestion window at the same rate as standard TCP. It should reduce its rate earlier as queues build, but it may not yield to low-load traffic that causes no measurable queueing delay. The target limits the extra delay concurrent LEDBAT flows add.

The RFC notes a possible latecomer's advantage among LEDBAT flows: a new flow may mistake an existing queue for its base delay. It identifies network effects, parameter choices, filtering, and framing as areas requiring further experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: LEDBAT is designed to yield to heavily loaded flows, but low-rate traffic may not create a delay signal it can detect. The RFC lists several behaviors that still need testing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If delay estimates are manipulated to appear low and the target is made very large, LEDBAT can behave like standard TCP. A man-in-the-middle may also alter timestamps or reported delays to make a flow back off when there is no congestion.

A protocol using LEDBAT should authenticate timestamps in data packets and delay values in acknowledgements. The RFC says LEDBAT is not known to introduce new privacy or integrity concerns and is compatible with IPsec and TLS or DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who changes timestamps or delay reports can affect the sending rate. Protocols using LEDBAT should authenticate those values.
